newsitem.title: FRANCE: Vasseur sees no fodder risk today in France.
newsitem.headline: Vasseur sees no fodder risk today in France.

text.p: French farm minister Philippe Vasseur said on Wednesday there was no risk today of suspect animal feed entering France illicitly, although there was evidence of fraud in the past.

Asked in an interview on Radio RTL if there was still a risk of illicit bonemeal imports, Vasseur said: "Today, no...I believe that today one can trust customs and fraud services to carry out the necessary controls."
Vasseur spoke after a French deputy heading a parliamentary probe into mad cow disease said on Tuesday that suspect animal feed had entered France in violation of restrictions in the past.

Jean-Francois Mattei, author of an unpublished report on the findings of a committee set up by the National Assembly, said lack of coordination between French authorities made it impossible to assess the scope of suspected fraud.

The recycling of animal parts such as bonemeal into feed is suspected to be the main cause of the spread of the disease, bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE), to thousands of British cattle from the 1980s onwards.
Britain prompted a Europe-wide health scare last year by announcing that infected beef might also cause the fatal brain disorder Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease (CJD) in humans.
France banned imports of the British feed in 1989.
Mattei said the report, which has not been released, criticised the handling of the disease on a European scale.

Vasseur told RTL that the European Union was still lagging in its response to the mad cow crisis. "It is true that there are gaps in European practice -- gaps that existed in the past and gaps that unfortunately still exist," he said

"At the European level, on the issue of removing certain components from the production of animal feed or on imposing mandatory labelling, Europe may have not drawn all the lessons from the crisis," he said.
